title: Whatchamacallit: being indirect
subtitle: the thing is, thingummy, loads of, no offence intended
summary: Use the vague, indirect language of informal speech - thing and get, thingummy and whatsisname, loads of and umpteen - and soften criticism so it does not offend.

lesson.heading: Vague and general words: thing
rows: That's one of the things I want to talk to him about.
thing = subject
Laura has got a thing about mice.
she either really likes or really dislikes them; is obsessed with them
Don't make such a big thing of it!
Don't make so much fuss about it!
There wasn't a thing we could do about it.
a thing = anything
For one thing, I haven't got time. For another thing, I can't afford it.
Firstly ..., secondly ...
The thing is, I have to take my car for a service tomorrow.
used to introduce a topic, a problem or an explanation
As things are at present, ...
as the situation is

lesson.heading: Vague and general words: get
lesson.text: **Get** does an enormous amount of work in informal speech. It can mean understand, send, organise, or simply manage to be somewhere.

examples.text: We must **get** that parcel in the post today.
She had big plans to travel the world but she just never **got it together**.

examples.note: = organise things so that the problem is solved

examples.text: I hope I can **get her to myself** this evening.

lesson.heading: When you can't think of the word
lesson.text: When we cannot remember a word or name, we replace it with a vague word. For objects: **thingy**, **thingummy**, **thingumijig**, **thingamibob**, **whatsit**, **whatchamacallit**, **whatnot**. For people: **whatsisname** for a man and **whatsername** for a woman - though **thingy** works for either.

examples.text: Have you seen the **thingy** we use for keeping the door open?
I was talking to **thingy** about that yesterday.
I need a **whatchamacallit** - you know, one of those things for flattening pastry.

lesson.note: These words can be spelt in several different ways.

lesson.heading: Informal quantifiers
rows: a lot of
bags of, a load of, loads of, a mass of, masses of, dozens of, tons of, umpteen
I can help you - I've got bags of time.
a lot of (money)
loads of
They can afford expensive holidays as they've got loads of money.
a lot of (times)
umpteen
I've tried phoning her umpteen times but she never answers.
a little, some
a bit of, a scrap of
I've got a bit of a headache. / You haven't done a scrap of work.
lesson.note: These quantifiers are common in informal speech but rare in formal writing.

lesson.heading: Being indirect and less threatening
rows: It's not the most practical/sensible/intelligent/appropriate thing you've ever done.
a gentle way of saying it is impractical, unwise, unintelligent or inappropriate
and I mean that in the nicest possible way
softens a criticism you have just made
No offence intended, but ...
warns that what follows may sound rude, and asks the listener not to take it badly
If you don't mind me/my saying so, ...
introduces a criticism politely
I gather (that) ...
I have heard it from someone
Incidentally, ...
introduces a new subject into the conversation in an indirect way
present company excepted
not including the people here
myself included
including me

lesson.heading: Softening in action
lesson.text: Put together, these expressions let you criticise almost anything without giving offence. Notice how each one takes the sting out of the sentence around it.

examples.text: **No offence intended**, but I think you've misunderstood the basic problem.
**If you don't mind my saying so**, I think that you could have handled that better.
What a load of idiots - **present company excepted**, of course.
The staff here, **myself included**, have not been working quite as hard as we should.

lesson.text: Thingy, whatsit and loads of belong to talk between friends - keep them out of essays and business letters.

exercises.prompt: 'Don't make such a big thing about it. I'm only going for a few days.' What does the speaker mean?
options: Don't make such a fuss about it.
Don't worry about the size of it.
exercises.explanation: To make a big thing of something is to make a lot of fuss about it.

exercises.prompt: 'Jess has got a thing about wanting straight hair.' What does this mean?
exercises.explanation: To have a thing about something is to really like or really dislike it - to be obsessed with it.

exercises.prompt: 'Did you get what the lecturer was saying? I didn't get a thing.' What does get mean here?
exercises.explanation: I didn't get a thing means I didn't understand anything.

exercises.prompt: The ___ is, I don't know when we'll be at home.
exercises.explanation: The thing is introduces a topic, a problem or an explanation.

exercises.prompt: I hope we can get everything sorted out today. It's time we got it ___ !
exercises.explanation: To get it together is to take positive action or organise yourself.

exercises.prompt: I don't get on with them very well. For one thing, we like different things. For ___ , I find them quite rude.
exercises.explanation: For one thing ... For another (thing) ... means firstly ... secondly ...

exercises.prompt: The speaker cannot think of the word. Match each sentence with the word they are looking for.

pairs.left: Where's the thingummy for sifting the flour?
Look, isn't that whatsisname? The actor who was in the latest James Bond?
I can't find the thingumijig for measuring angles.
Have you got a whatsit, you know, for bashing in nails?
Where's the thingy for draining potatoes?
I need a whatchamacallit for flattening pastry.

exercises.prompt: Which vague word would you use for a woman whose name you cannot remember?
exercises.explanation: Whatsisname is used for a man and whatsername for a woman; thingy works for either.

exercises.prompt: Make it informal: He hasn't done any useful work here since he first got the job. He hasn't done ___ useful work here since he first got the job.
exercises.explanation: A scrap of means a little or, in a negative sentence, none at all.

exercises.prompt: Make it informal: I've asked her out a great many times, but she's always got some excuse. I've asked her out ___ times.
exercises.explanation: Umpteen is an informal way of saying a very large number of.

exercises.prompt: Make it informal: Yasmin's got a great deal of energy. Yasmin's got ___ energy!
exercises.explanation: Bags of, loads of and tons of are all informal ways of saying a lot of.

exercises.prompt: This is a very boring party, present ___ excepted, of course.
exercises.explanation: Present company excepted means not including the people here.

exercises.prompt: No one, myself ___ , seems to be making much of an effort to chat.
exercises.explanation: Myself included adds the speaker to the criticism, which softens it.

exercises.prompt: I ___ a lot of people couldn't come.
exercises.explanation: I gather that ... means I have heard it from someone.

exercises.prompt: ___ , no offence intended, but don't you think you could have dressed a bit more smartly?
exercises.explanation: Incidentally is often used to introduce a new subject into the conversation in an indirect way.

exercises.prompt: If you don't ___ me saying so, I think you should have changed out of your gardening clothes.
exercises.explanation: If you don't mind me/my saying so introduces a criticism politely.

exercises.prompt: I mean that in the nicest ___ way, of course!
exercises.explanation: And I mean that in the nicest possible way softens the criticism just made.

exercises.statement: Saying 'It's not the most sensible thing you've ever done' is a softened way of saying it was rather unwise.
exercises.explanation: Correct - this negative pattern lets you criticise without sounding aggressive.

exercises.prompt: Does each expression mean a lot, or a little?
